Building models sequentially to improve a combined prediction.
A setting chosen before or during the training setup.
beginner.activity: Two models disagree. Does using both automatically guarantee the right answer?
beginner.answer: No. Evaluate the combined model on unseen examples.

chapters.title: k-NN & K-Means Clustering
chapters.summary: Distance-based classification and discovering hidden data clusters.

sections.title: k-Nearest Neighbors (k-NN)
sections.body:
k-Nearest Neighbors (k-NN) is arguably the simplest algorithm in all of machine learning. Unlike neural networks or regression, k-NN doesn't actually 'learn' any mathematical equation at all. In fact, its training phase is literally just saving the dataset into memory. Because of this, it is called a 'lazy learning' algorithm.

When a new data point comes in for inference, the algorithm calculates the geometric distance (usually Euclidean) between that new point and every single point in the historical database. It then looks at the 'k' closest points. If you set k=5, it finds the 5 closest historical examples. Those 5 neighbors cast a vote based on their labels, and the majority wins.

While incredibly simple to implement, k-NN scales terribly in production. If you have 10 million users in your database, classifying a single new user requires calculating 10 million distances on the fly. This makes it incredibly slow for high-throughput backend APIs, though it remains a powerful baseline tool for small datasets and recommendation engines.
keyPoints: k-NN classifies new data by finding the most similar historical examples and voting.
It has zero training time but extremely slow inference time on large datasets.
The value 'k' is a hyperparameter—always use an odd number to avoid tie votes.
sections.example: If a real estate app wants to estimate the price of your house, a k-NN model simply finds the 5 houses geographically closest to yours with similar square footage (the 5 nearest neighbors) and averages their recent sale prices.
sections.misconception: Common mistake: Choosing an even number for 'k' in binary classification. If you set k=4, you risk a 2-2 tie vote. Always set 'k' to an odd number (like 3, 5, or 7) to guarantee a majority winner.
sections.analogy: Think of it like moving to a new city and trying to figure out if your neighborhood is conservative or liberal. You don't read the city charter; you just knock on the doors of your 5 closest neighbors and ask them. The majority vote is your answer.

sections.title: K-Means: Grouping Without Labels
sections.body:
So far, we have discussed 'Supervised Learning', where you have a Label (y) like 'Spam' or 'Price' to train against. K-Means belongs to 'Unsupervised Learning'. In this scenario, you just have a massive database of user behavior, but no labels. You ask the algorithm: 'I don't know what the patterns are, but please divide my users into exactly K distinct groups based on their similarities.'

K-Means works through an elegant, repetitive dance. If you want 3 groups (K=3), the algorithm drops 3 random center points (centroids) into the data space. First, every data point assigns itself to the closest centroid. Second, the algorithm recalculates the exact center of those new clusters, and moves the centroid to that exact middle.

It repeats this process—assign points, move centroid, assign points, move centroid—until the centroids stop moving entirely. The result is a mathematically optimized segmentation of your data, heavily used in marketing to automatically discover distinct customer personas.
keyPoints: K-Means is unsupervised learning; it finds hidden groupings in data without labels.
You must manually specify the number of clusters (K) before running the algorithm.
The algorithm alternates between assigning points and centering clusters until stable.
sections.example: A marketing team at Nike feeds millions of customer purchase histories into a K-Means model with K=4. Without human input, the model outputs 4 distinct clusters: 'Weekend Runners', 'Yoga Enthusiasts', 'Sneakerheads', and 'Bargain Hunters', allowing for highly targeted email campaigns.
sections.misconception: Common mistake: Assuming K-Means will automatically figure out the optimal number of groups. If you tell it to find 100 groups in data that only has 2 natural segments, it will brutally slice the data into 100 meaningless pieces.
sections.analogy: Think of it like an elementary school teacher telling 30 kids on a playground to 'form 3 groups based on who you are closest to'. The kids shuffle around, gravitate toward three hubs, and eventually settle into three tight circles without any explicit rules.

sections.title: Why Feature Scaling Matters
sections.body:
Any algorithm that relies on calculating spatial distance between data points—such as k-NN, K-Means, or Support Vector Machines—contains a massive pitfall for new engineers: the dominance of large numbers. If you don't scale your features, the algorithm will mathematically ignore your most important data.

Imagine you have a dataset of users with two features: Age (ranging from 18 to 70) and Annual Salary (ranging from $20,000 to $150,000). When the algorithm calculates the distance between two users, the mathematical difference in their salaries might be $40,000, while the difference in their age is only 5 years. Because $40,000 is infinitely larger than 5, the geometry of the algorithm will be 99.9% dominated by Salary. It essentially treats Age as if it doesn't exist.

To fix this, developers must apply Feature Scaling (like Min-Max Normalization or Standard Scaling) before training. Normalization crushes every single column down so all values fall strictly between 0 and 1. Suddenly, Age and Salary are on the exact same playing field, and the algorithm can respect both features equally.
keyPoints: Distance-based algorithms mathematically over-prioritize columns with massive numeric values.
Feature scaling transforms all columns to a uniform scale (e.g., between 0 and 1).
Without scaling, small-number columns (like Age) are entirely ignored by the model.
sections.example: If a hospital uses K-Means to group patients based on 'White Blood Cell Count' (measured in thousands) and 'Body Temperature' (measured around 98.6), the algorithm will completely ignore the fever data unless both metrics are normalized to a 0-1 scale.
sections.misconception: Common mistake: Applying scaling to the training set, but forgetting to apply the exact same scaling logic to new live data in production. If your model expects numbers between 0-1 and the API sends a raw salary of $80,000, the model will crash or produce garbage output.
sections.analogy: Think of it like mixing a cocktail. If the recipe calls for '1 part bitters and 1 part soda', but you measure the bitters in drops and the soda in gallons, the drink is ruined. Scaling ensures all ingredients are measured using the exact same unit.

chapters.example:
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

# Always scale before computing distance!
X_scaled = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X)
kmeans = KMeans(n_clusters=3, random_state=42)
clusters = kmeans.fit_predict(X_scaled)
chapters.exercise: If you double k in k-NN from 1 to 21, does the decision boundary become more jagged or smoother?
chapters.answer: Smoother! Larger k considers a broader neighborhood, reducing noise sensitivity and smoothing the boundary.

checks.question: Why must you scale features before running k-NN or K-Means?
options: Otherwise large-magnitude features dominate distance calculations
Scaling is required by Python syntax
checks.explanation: Distance formulas (like Euclidean) are heavily biased towards features with large numbers.

checks.question: What kind of learning is K-Means clustering?
checks.explanation: K-Means discovers natural clusters without predefined target labels.

beginner.prerequisite: Start with features; distances and averages help.
beginner.plain: Find similar examples. k-NN predicts using neighbours; K-Means groups data.
terms: A nearby example under a chosen distance measure.
A group of examples treated as similar.
Adjusting numerical inputs so their units do not dominate distance.
beginner.activity: Would grouping parcels by weight necessarily reveal their delivery destinations?
beginner.answer: No. Groups reflect the chosen inputs; they do not automatically have the meaning you want.

chapters.title: Evaluation & Overfitting
chapters.summary: Train/Val/Test splits, precision, recall, and debugging generalisation.

sections.title: The Golden Rule: Never Test on Training Data
sections.body:
The single most catastrophic mistake an engineer can make in machine learning is evaluating a model's performance on the exact same data it was trained on. Modern algorithms, especially neural networks and deep decision trees, possess enough mathematical capacity to simply memorize the entire dataset.

If you show a model a set of flashcards, and then test it using the exact same flashcards, a 100% score doesn't mean the model is intelligent—it means it has a good memory. If you deploy that model to production to face data it has never seen before, it will fail miserably. This is the definition of overfitting.

To prevent this, engineers strictly partition their database before any code is run. The standard practice is a three-way split: 70% Training data (the flashcards to learn from), 15% Validation data (used iteratively to tune hyperparameter settings), and 15% Test data. The Test data is locked away in a digital vault and is evaluated exactly once at the very end of the project. This ensures your final accuracy metric represents true, real-world generalization.
keyPoints: Testing on training data provides a dangerously false sense of high accuracy.
Always split data into Training, Validation, and Test sets before starting.
The Test set must be kept entirely hidden until the final model is fully locked.
sections.example: An engineer at a startup boasts their new stock-prediction model has 99% accuracy. However, they tested it on data from 2020—the exact same data they used to train it. When deployed in 2024, the model loses money immediately because it only memorized 2020 market quirks, never the underlying logic.
sections.misconception: Common mistake: Tuning your model's hyperparameters to improve the Test set score repeatedly. By doing this, you are manually leaking the Test set's answers into the model. Hyperparameters must be tuned exclusively on the Validation set.
sections.analogy: Think of it like a college professor teaching a math course. The Training data is the homework. The Validation data is the practice exam. The Test data is the final exam. If the professor puts the exact homework questions on the final exam, grades reflect memorization, not math skills.

sections.title: Accuracy is Dangerous on Imbalanced Data
sections.body:
When developers evaluate a model, their first instinct is always to check the 'Accuracy' metric—simply the percentage of predictions the model got right. But in real-world business scenarios, Accuracy is often a dangerously misleading vanity metric that hides a completely broken system. This happens anytime your dataset is 'imbalanced'.

Imagine you are building a fraud detection model for Visa. In reality, 99.9% of all credit card swipes are perfectly legitimate, and only 0.1% are actual fraud. A totally useless machine learning model could just hardcode: return 'Legitimate'. This brain-dead model would technically achieve 99.9% accuracy, completely fooling executives, while letting every single fraudulent transaction pass through.

When one class heavily outnumbers the other, accuracy breaks down. Engineers must completely abandon it and use advanced metrics like the Confusion Matrix, Precision, Recall, and the F1-Score to understand how the model is actually behaving on the rare, important minority class.
keyPoints: Accuracy is only reliable when your classes are roughly a 50/50 split.
On imbalanced datasets, a model can guess the majority class and achieve 99% accuracy while failing its purpose.
Business-critical events (fraud, cancer, churn) are almost always highly imbalanced.
sections.example: A hospital builds an AI to detect a rare genetic disease that affects 1 in 1,000 people. The model proudly reports 99.9% accuracy. The doctors are thrilled, until they realize the model achieves this by simply telling every single patient they are perfectly healthy.
sections.misconception: Common mistake: Reporting overall accuracy to stakeholders when dealing with churn prediction, fraud detection, or disease screening. You must report metrics on the positive class specifically to avoid disaster.
sections.analogy: Think of it like a broken clock stuck at 3:00. It is perfectly accurate twice a day. A machine learning model that always predicts the majority class is the same broken clock—technically accurate, but fundamentally useless.

sections.title: Precision vs Recall Tradeoff
sections.body:
Once you abandon standard Accuracy, you must judge your model using two competing metrics: Precision and Recall. Precision answers the question: 'Out of all the times the model sounded the alarm, how often was it actually a real fire?' High precision means very few false alarms (False Positives). Recall answers a totally different question: 'Out of all the real fires that actually happened, how many did the model successfully detect?' High recall means you missed very few real threats (False Negatives).

Here is the painful reality of machine learning in production: you almost never get both. Precision and Recall are mathematically opposed. If you increase the sensitivity of your model to catch every possible positive case (Recall up), you will inevitably start flagging innocent cases too (Precision down). This tradeoff is real, unavoidable, and must be managed by adjusting the decision threshold.

The F1-Score is the harmonic mean of Precision and Recall, giving a single number that balances both. Use it when you need to compare two models that have different Precision/Recall tradeoffs. In high-stakes domains, engineers often explicitly state a business target: 'We require at least 90% Recall, and will accept whatever Precision that gives us'.
keyPoints: Precision measures the accuracy of positive predictions (avoiding false alarms).
Recall measures the completeness of positive detection (avoiding missed threats).
Improving one metric almost always hurts the other—choose based on business cost.
sections.example: A radiologist AI at Johns Hopkins scanning X-rays for tumors is tuned for maximum Recall (0.99). It will flag 50 patients who don't have cancer (low Precision) to guarantee it never misses a patient who does. The cost of a false alarm is a follow-up scan; the cost of a miss is a death.
sections.misconception: Common mistake: Optimizing for F1-Score alone without asking which error is more costly in your domain. In many business contexts, a False Negative is 10x more costly than a False Positive, and a pure F1 optimization would ignore this entirely.
sections.analogy: Think of it like a fishing net. A tiny-mesh net (high Recall) catches every single fish, but also catches rocks, seaweed, and boots. A large-mesh net (high Precision) only catches real fish, but lets smaller fish escape. The mesh size is your decision threshold.

chapters.example:
from sklearn.metrics import classification_report, confusion_matrix

# Inspect precision, recall, and f1-score
print(confusion_matrix(y_true, y_pred))
print(classification_report(y_true, y_pred, target_names=["Legit", "Fraud"]))
chapters.exercise: In an airport security weapon detector, do you prioritize Precision or Recall?
chapters.answer: Recall! A false alarm (low precision) means an extra bag search; a missed weapon (low recall) is catastrophic.

checks.question: A fraud detector predicts no fraud ever on a dataset with 1% fraud. What is its Recall for fraud?
checks.explanation: It found 0 out of the actual fraud cases, so recall is 0% despite 99% accuracy.

checks.question: Which dataset split should be held out and evaluated only once at the very end?
checks.explanation: The test set gives an unbiased estimate of real-world generalization.

beginner.prerequisite: Start with Meet Machine Learning and Classification.
beginner.plain: Test on examples the model did not learn from.
terms: Examples reserved for a final evaluation.
Learning training details that do not generalize well.
A simple approach used as a comparison.
beginner.activity: Only 1 of 100 parcels is late. A model always says “on time”. Is 99% accuracy enough?
beginner.answer: No. It misses every late parcel. The useful metric depends on the mistakes that matter.

chapters.title: Generative AI & Clear Prompts
chapters.summary: Understand what a language model does, then practise giving it a clear request.

sections.title: What does generative AI generate?
sections.body:
Generative AI produces content such as text, images, or audio using patterns learned during training. A large language model (LLM) works with text represented as small pieces called tokens. A token may be part of a word.

A prompt is the request and information you give the model. The model uses this context to produce a response. A fluent response can contain mistakes, so check important claims against reliable evidence.
sections.example: A delivery model predicts “30 minutes”. A generative model drafts a message explaining the delay.
keyPoints: Generative AI creates content.
An LLM processes text in tokens.
A convincing answer is not proof of accuracy.

sections.title: Give a task, context, and a useful format
sections.body:
Start by saying what you need. Add relevant information, the intended reader, and the desired format. If the model should use only an attached passage, say so and ask it to flag missing information.

You can show examples of a good answer. This is called few-shot prompting. It provides examples in the current context; it does not retrain the model. Try your prompt on several inputs, including difficult ones.
sections.example: Vague: “Explain AI.” Clearer: “Explain machine learning to someone with no coding experience. Use a parcel-delivery example and three short bullet points.”
keyPoints: State a concrete task.
Provide relevant context and an output format.
Examples can help, but results still need checking.

sections.title: Instructions guide; checks verify
sections.body:
Applications may provide system instructions to guide the model across a conversation. These instructions are not a guarantee that every response will follow the rules. Software must enforce permissions and validate any action.

JSON is a text format with named fields that software can read. Some model services support structured output with a schema, which describes the expected fields. A valid format can still contain incorrect values.

For a difficult task, break it into smaller steps and check the result. Asking for a brief explanation can help you assess an answer, but a model does not need to expose its private reasoning to give a useful response.
sections.example: A response like {"minutes": 30} is easy for software to read. The app must still check that 30 is a supported estimate.
keyPoints: Prompts are not permission controls.
Structured output helps with format, not factual truth.
Check the answer rather than assuming a longer explanation is better.

chapters.example:
# A prompt you can copy into a text assistant
prompt = """Explain machine learning to a beginner.
Use a parcel-delivery example.
Return three short bullet points.
Define any technical words you use."""
# This stores text; it does not call a model.
chapters.exercise: Rewrite “Help with my homework” into a specific request for a hint, without asking for the final answer.
chapters.answer: For example: “I am learning averages. For the numbers 4, 6, and 8, give me one hint about the first step. Do not calculate the answer yet.”

checks.question: What does a few-shot prompt include?
options: Examples of useful inputs and outputs
checks.explanation: Examples show the desired pattern inside the current prompt; the model is not retrained.

checks.question: A model returns correctly formatted JSON. What should the app do next?
options: Check the values and permissions before using them
Assume the model has learned permanently
checks.explanation: Correct formatting does not establish accuracy or authorization.

beginner.prerequisite: No coding needed. Start from zero introduces the vocabulary.
beginner.plain: Ask for content with a clear task, relevant context, and a useful format.
terms: Large language model: a model that processes and generates text.
A piece of text a model processes, sometimes part of a word.
The instructions and context supplied to a model.
beginner.activity: Rewrite “Explain deliveries” for a child who wants to know why a parcel is late.
beginner.answer: “Explain three possible reasons a parcel is late to a ten-year-old. Use short sentences and say these are possibilities, not confirmed causes.”

chapters.title: Vector Embeddings & Semantic Search
chapters.summary: Turning text into geometric vectors and searching by meaning, not keywords.

sections.title: Text as High-Dimensional Vectors
sections.body:
Computers do not understand English. They cannot comprehend concepts, emotion, or meaning. To make an AI understand text, we must translate words into the only thing computers do understand: numbers. This translation process is done via an 'Embedding Model'.

An embedding model acts as a massive mathematical dictionary. You pass in a word, a sentence, or an entire document, and it outputs a dense array of floating-point numbers—usually around 1,536 numbers long. This array is called a Vector. These numbers aren't random; they represent the semantic coordinates of that text in a high-dimensional space.

The genius of the embedding space is that distance equals meaning. The model is trained so that concepts with similar semantic meanings are mathematically pushed close together, while unrelated concepts are pushed far apart. Therefore, an AI doesn't need to 'know' what a dog is; it just knows that the vector for 'dog' is mathematically sitting right next to the vectors for 'puppy', 'bark', and 'pet'.
keyPoints: Embedding models convert unstructured text into arrays of numbers called vectors.
These vectors represent the exact coordinates of a concept in high-dimensional space.
Similar concepts are mathematically clustered close together, enabling semantic understanding.
sections.example: If you embed the words 'King', 'Queen', 'Apple', and 'Banana', the computer doesn't know what fruit or royalty is. But in the vector space, the coordinates for King and Queen will be tightly clustered in one corner, while Apple and Banana are clustered far away in another. The famous equation 'King - Man + Woman ≈ Queen' comes directly from this geometry.
sections.misconception: Common mistake: Thinking embeddings just match exact keywords. If you embed 'Canine' and 'Dog', they might not share a single letter, but their numerical vectors will be nearly identical because their underlying meaning is the same.
sections.analogy: Think of it like GPS coordinates for concepts. If 'New York' is at [40.7, -74.0] and 'Boston' is at [42.3, -71.0], they are close together. Embeddings just add 1,500 more coordinates to map out exactly where a concept lives in the universe of human language.

sections.title: Cosine Similarity & Semantic Distance
sections.body:
Once you have converted all your company's documents into numerical vectors, how do you actually search through them? In traditional SQL databases, you search using exact string matches or regex. In the AI world, you search using a geometric formula called Cosine Similarity.

Cosine similarity measures the mathematical angle between two vectors in space. When a user types a search query like 'how to reset my password', you first run that query through the embedding model to get its vector. Then, you calculate the cosine angle between the query vector and every single document vector in your database.

If the angle between two vectors is 0 degrees, their cosine similarity is 1.0 (a perfect semantic match). If they point in completely opposite directions, the score drops toward 0. Because this relies entirely on geometric angles rather than text matching, a user can search for 'I lost my login credentials' and perfectly retrieve a document titled 'Password Recovery Guide', even though they share literally zero words.
keyPoints: Cosine similarity is the mathematical engine behind AI semantic search.
It calculates the angle between a user's query vector and document vectors.
A score close to 1.0 means highly relevant; a score closer to 0 means unrelated.
sections.example: A customer searches a help desk for 'My screen is totally cracked'. A keyword search fails because the repair manual says 'Display shatter replacement'. Cosine similarity easily connects the two because 'cracked screen' and 'shattered display' point in the exact same mathematical direction in embedding space.
sections.misconception: Common mistake: Using standard Euclidean distance (straight-line distance) instead of Cosine distance for text embeddings. Euclidean distance gets confused by document length—a 10-page document looks mathematically far from a 1-sentence query—whereas Cosine purely measures the angle of meaning, ignoring length entirely.
sections.analogy: Think of it like pointing telescopes at the night sky. If you and I are both looking at the same star, our telescopes are pointing at the exact same angle (high cosine similarity), regardless of whether you have a massive observatory telescope and I have cheap binoculars.

sections.title: Vector Databases (Chroma, Pinecone, FAISS)
sections.body:
While calculating cosine similarity is mathematically simple for a few documents, it becomes an infrastructure nightmare at scale. If your company has 10 million embedded documents, and a user submits a search query, your server has to instantly calculate the geometric angle against all 10 million arrays of 1,500 floating-point numbers. A standard SQL database like Postgres will grind to a halt trying to compute this sequentially.

To solve this, the industry created a new piece of infrastructure: the Vector Database. Technologies like Pinecone, Chroma, and FAISS are specifically engineered to store and search high-dimensional floating-point arrays.

Instead of checking every single document, Vector DBs use advanced indexing algorithms—most notably HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World). HNSW builds a massive, multi-layered graph of your vectors. When a search query enters, it rapidly navigates through the network of nearest neighbors, skipping millions of irrelevant vectors entirely. This allows you to find the top 5 most relevant documents out of billions, in less than 50 milliseconds.
keyPoints: Standard relational databases cannot efficiently compute vector distances at massive scale.
Vector Databases are purpose-built infrastructure for storing and querying AI embeddings.
They use algorithms like HNSW to rapidly approximate the closest matches in milliseconds.
sections.example: When you ask Notion AI a question, it doesn't send your entire workspace to the LLM. It takes your question, queries a vector database, retrieves the 3 most geometrically similar paragraphs from your thousands of notes in under 20 milliseconds, and uses only those to answer.
sections.misconception: Common mistake: Thinking you have to migrate your entire data architecture to a Vector DB. You usually keep your source-of-truth text in Postgres or AWS S3, and just use the Vector DB as an auxiliary search index, storing only the vectors and a reference ID.
sections.analogy: Think of it like looking for a specific book in a massive library. A standard database checks every single book on every single shelf sequentially. A Vector DB is like a hyper-efficient librarian who immediately walks to the correct wing, then the correct aisle, zeroing in on the book instantly.

chapters.exercise: Why does semantic vector search beat traditional keyword search for a customer support bot?
chapters.answer: Users use different vocabulary (e.g., "my bill is broken" vs "invoice discrepancy"). Vector search matches the underlying intent.

checks.question: What does an embedding model output for a given sentence?
options: A fixed-length vector of floating-point numbers
checks.explanation: Embeddings represent text as continuous vectors in a semantic geometric space.

checks.question: Which metric is standard for measuring similarity between two normalized text embeddings?
checks.explanation: Cosine similarity measures the angle between vectors, capturing semantic closeness.

beginner.prerequisite: Read Generative AI & Clear Prompts first.
beginner.plain: Represent text as lists of numbers so related meanings can be compared.
terms: A numerical representation of an item.
Searching by meaning rather than only exact words.
beginner.activity: Could “Where is my parcel?” match a document titled “Track your shipment”?
beginner.answer: Yes. Their meanings are related even though the words differ. Similarity still needs checking.

chapters.title: RAG: Retrieval-Augmented Generation
chapters.summary: Help a model answer from relevant documents, and check whether the answer is supported.

sections.title: Give the model something to look up
sections.body:
A language model can generate a plausible answer even when the information it needs is missing. An incorrect or unsupported generated claim is often called a hallucination.

If you ask about a shop’s return policy, the model needs the actual policy. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) supplies relevant material at the time of the question instead of relying only on what the model learned during training.
sections.example: Question: “Can I return an opened item?” First find the shop’s current returns policy.
keyPoints: A model may be wrong even when it sounds certain.
Retrieve relevant evidence before generating an answer.
Check that documents are current and appropriate for the user.

sections.title: Find, provide, answer
sections.body:
A simple RAG system has three steps. Retrieve relevant passages from a collection. Put those passages and the question into the model’s context. Ask the model to answer using the passages and identify the source.

Retrieval can use keyword search, meaning-based search with embeddings, or a combination. A vector database is one possible implementation, not a requirement.
sections.example: A policy says “Unopened items may be returned within 14 days.” If it says nothing about opened items, the answer should acknowledge that gap.
keyPoints: Retrieve passages relevant to the question.
Include the passages in the prompt.
Ask for sources and allow “not enough information”.

sections.title: Check the search and the answer separately
sections.body:
When an answer is wrong, inspect the retrieved passages first. Did the search find the right document? Then compare the answer with that document. Does the source actually support each important claim?

RAG can reduce unsupported answers, but it does not eliminate them. Test cases with missing evidence, conflicting policies, and outdated documents. Only retrieve material the user is allowed to see.
sections.example: Finding the right policy but inventing a 30-day window is an answer error. Finding an unrelated shipping policy is a retrieval error.
keyPoints: Search quality and answer quality are different checks.
A citation can still fail to support a claim.
Missing evidence should lead to uncertainty, not an invented answer.

chapters.example:
def rag_answer(user_query):
    # 1. Retrieve top matching chunks
    context_chunks = vector_db.search(user_query, top_k=3)
    
    # 2. Augment prompt with retrieved ground truth
    prompt = f"Answer using ONLY this context:\n{context_chunks}\n\nQuestion: {user_query}"
    
    # 3. Generate grounded response
    return llm.generate(prompt)
chapters.exercise: A company policy manual updates every week. Why is RAG superior to fine-tuning the model every week?
chapters.answer: Retrieval lets you update the document collection without retraining model weights. You still need to refresh the search index where applicable, enforce access permissions, and evaluate answers.

checks.question: What is the primary role of Retrieval in a RAG pipeline?
options: To fetch relevant external facts to include in the context window
checks.explanation: Retrieval supplies relevant, up-to-date document chunks into the prompt context.

checks.question: If an LLM gives an answer unsupported by retrieved context, what is this called?
checks.explanation: Hallucination is when a model generates claims unsupported by factual evidence.

beginner.prerequisite: Read the prompting and embeddings lessons first.
beginner.plain: Look up relevant information before asking a model to answer.
terms: Retrieval-augmented generation: answer with retrieved context.
Finding relevant information in a collection.
Supporting an answer with supplied evidence.
beginner.activity: A policy describes unopened returns only. Can you conclude that opened items are accepted?
beginner.answer: No. The evidence does not answer that question. Say what is missing.

chapters.title: Fine-Tuning vs RAG vs In-Context
chapters.summary: Choose between clearer instructions, document retrieval, and additional model training.

sections.title: Start with a prompt and a test
sections.body:
Prompting gives a model instructions, context, and examples at the time you use it. It is often a useful first experiment because you can change the request without retraining.

Create a small set of representative tasks and decide what a good answer looks like. Compare revisions on the same tasks. Prompts still require testing and maintenance; longer inputs may increase cost and delay.
sections.example: Try three example summaries to show the style you want, then evaluate on documents that were not among those examples.
keyPoints: Start with a measurable task.
Try clear instructions and examples.
Keep separate examples for evaluation.

sections.title: Use retrieval for information you need to look up
sections.body:
Retrieval supplies relevant external information, such as current policies or product listings. It is useful when information changes, when sources matter, or when the collection is too large to include in each prompt.

You can combine retrieval with prompting or a fine-tuned model. These are complementary tools, not fixed levels that everyone must climb.
sections.example: For current opening hours, look up the latest shop listing instead of expecting a model to remember it.
keyPoints: Retrieve changing information.
Keep source permissions and freshness in mind.
Check whether retrieved evidence supports the answer.

sections.title: Fine-tuning is additional training
sections.body:
Fine-tuning updates a model using selected training examples. It can improve task performance, style, or output behaviour, but it needs suitable data and evaluation. It can also make some capabilities worse.

LoRA, short for low-rank adaptation, trains a smaller set of added parameters while keeping the original parameters fixed. This can reduce training resource needs. The required hardware, data, and time depend on the model and task.
sections.example: If a tested prompt still handles a repeated classification task poorly, compare a fine-tuned model on a held-out set before deciding it helps.
keyPoints: Fine-tuning changes learned parameters.
LoRA is one way to make that training more efficient.
An improvement on training examples is not enough.

chapters.example:
# DECISION MATRIX:
# Need new facts / changing docs? -> Use RAG
# Need specific tone / complex formatting / lower latency? -> Fine-Tune (LoRA)
# Need quick prototype / few examples? -> In-Context Prompting
chapters.exercise: A shop needs answers about opening hours that change every week. What would you try first?
chapters.answer: Retrieve the current shop listing and provide it to the model. Test that the answer matches the listing and admits when information is absent.

checks.question: Which method updates learned model parameters?
options: Adding a document to the prompt
checks.explanation: Fine-tuning performs additional training; prompting and retrieval provide information at use time.

checks.question: What should determine whether fine-tuning helped?
options: Performance on separate representative test examples
The number of training runs alone
A guarantee from the training method
checks.explanation: Evaluate on examples held out from training and compare with the original approach.

beginner.prerequisite: Read prompting, RAG, and evaluation; optional deeper topic.
beginner.plain: Choose a method based on what your tests show is missing.
terms: Additional training that updates learned parameters.
A learned numerical value inside a model.
A method that trains added low-rank parameter matrices.
beginner.activity: Opening hours change every week. Would you first retrain or retrieve the current listing?
beginner.answer: Retrieve the current listing, then check the answer against it.

chapters.title: AI Agents: Tools, Actions & Checks
chapters.summary: See how a model can use tools to work through a task, with clear limits.

sections.title: From answering to taking steps
sections.body:
A chatbot can suggest a plan. An agent system can also use tools and choose a next step based on the results. A tool might search a document collection or look up delivery status.

A typical cycle is: choose a step, request a tool, inspect the result, and continue or stop. A fixed workflow follows predefined steps; an agent gives the model more choice over what happens next. Use the simplest approach that works.
sections.example: To answer “Where is my parcel?”, a system can look up the tracking number, read the status, and explain it to you.
keyPoints: Tools connect the model to information or actions.
Observations can change the next step.
Not every task needs an agent.

sections.title: Tool requests need permission checks
sections.body:
Function calling lets a model request a named operation with arguments, such as lookup_parcel(tracking_id). An API is an interface that lets software request work from other software.

The host application decides whether to execute the request. It must check the user’s permissions and validate the arguments. Generating text does not make a tool request harmless: an application that executes it could change real data.

For consequential actions, such as sending a message or placing an order, build in an appropriate review or confirmation step.
sections.example: Looking up a parcel status is different from changing its delivery address. The second action needs stronger checks.
keyPoints: A tool request is not authorization.
Validate inputs and restrict access.
Treat tool output and retrieved text as potentially untrusted.

sections.title: Know when to stop
sections.body:
An agent should stop when its goal is reached, when it needs human help, or when it hits a limit. Set limits on steps, retries, time, and spending. Failed tools should produce a useful fallback, not an endless loop.

Model Context Protocol (MCP) standardizes connections to tools and data. It does not remove the need for setup, authentication, or permission checks. Multiple agents can divide work, but they also add coordination and failure points. Learn one reliable tool loop first.
sections.example: If a tracking service fails twice, report that the status could not be checked. Do not invent a delivery date or retry forever.
keyPoints: Define success and stopping conditions.
Set budgets and retry limits.
MCP and multiple agents are optional advanced topics.

chapters.example:
# Illustrative pseudocode: these functions must be implemented.
for step in range(5):
    request = choose_next_step(history)
    if request.needs_human or request.is_complete:
        break
    validate_arguments(request)
    check_user_permission(request)
    result = run_allowed_tool(request)
    history.append(result)
else:
    report_step_limit()
chapters.exercise: A parcel lookup tool keeps failing. Should the agent retry forever, invent a status, or stop with an explanation?
chapters.answer: Stop after a bounded number of retries and explain that the status could not be checked. Offer a next step such as trying again later.

checks.question: A model requests a tool that changes an address. What must happen before execution?
options: Execute because the request is valid JSON
Check arguments, permissions, and any required confirmation
checks.explanation: The application must enforce whether the requested action is allowed.

checks.question: What should an agent do after reaching its retry limit?
options: Stop and explain the failure or ask for help
checks.explanation: A bounded failure is preferable to an endless loop or an unsupported claim.

beginner.prerequisite: Read prompting and RAG first. Coding is optional for the explanation.
beginner.plain: Let a model request tools, inspect results, and stop within defined limits.
terms: A system where a model can choose steps and use tools toward a goal.
An operation made available to the model by an application.
An interface through which software requests information or actions.
beginner.activity: An agent can draft a reply. Does that automatically give it permission to send it?
beginner.answer: No. Drafting and sending are separate actions with separate permissions.

games.title: Draw the Boundary
games.description: Adjust a separating line and inspect its mistakes.
games.goal: Find a boundary that separates the two classes with high accuracy.

games.title: Overfitting Playground
games.description: Compare a flexible fit with the signal beneath the noise.
games.goal: Compare low, medium, and high flexibility. Explain why zero training error can mislead.

games.title: Threshold Tuner
games.description: Make a decision threshold visible through a confusion matrix.
games.goal: Reach at least 80% recall. Observe what happens to precision.

games.title: Gradient Descent
games.description: Take real gradient steps and see convergence or divergence.
games.goal: Reach a loss below 0.01 without diverging.

games.title: Cluster Detective
games.description: Step through assignment and centroid updates.
games.goal: Run iterations to convergence, then compare k = 2 and k = 3.

games.title: Iris Model Lab
games.description: Train and evaluate a classifier on published flower measurements.
games.goal: Compare k = 1, 5, and 15 on the fixed holdout. Inspect the confusion matrix.

challenges.question: A shop wants to predict next month’s sales.
options: Use a seasonal or recent-sales baseline and evaluate on later months.
Shuffle all months and evaluate training accuracy.
challenges.explanation: Time order matters. Future prediction needs a split that reflects the future.

challenges.question: Only 1% of messages are urgent. A model predicts “not urgent” every time.
options: Inspect urgent-case recall and precision, not just overall accuracy.
challenges.explanation: The system misses every urgent message. High accuracy hides that failure.

challenges.question: You have purchase histories but no segment labels.
options: Explore clustering after deciding how to represent similarity.
Claim discovered clusters are objectively true customer types.
challenges.explanation: Clustering explores structure; the representation and interpretation matter.

challenges.question: A default model uses collections status recorded after default.
options: Keep it because it improves accuracy.
Remove this future-derived feature and re-evaluate.
challenges.explanation: The information is unavailable at the intended prediction time.

challenges.question: A model memorises every training example.
options: Compare with a baseline on representative unseen data.
Assume more memory means better reasoning.
challenges.explanation: Generalisation, not memorisation, is the goal.

challenges.question: A handbook changes every week. Employees need supported answers.
options: Fine-tune once and assume the facts stay current.
Try permission-aware retrieval with answer-support evaluation.
challenges.explanation: Retrieval can supply changing documents; it still needs quality checks.

challenges.question: A distance model uses annual income and a 0–1 satisfaction score.
options: Investigate scaling within each training fold.
Scale using the whole dataset before splitting.
challenges.explanation: Magnitude can dominate distance. Learn transformations only on training data.

challenges.question: You have 3,000 labelled rows and limited compute.
options: Start with simple baselines and compare suitable tabular models.
challenges.explanation: The dataset, evaluation, and constraints should drive the choice.

challenges.question: An LLM returns unpredictable conversational responses when you need strict database JSON.
options: Enforce a structured JSON output schema and provide few-shot examples.
Add more exclamation points to the prompt.
challenges.explanation: Structured schema enforcement and few-shot formatting reliably constrain LLM output.

challenges.question: An autonomous AI agent gets stuck calling the same failing tool repeatedly.
options: Run the agent in an infinite loop.
Implement a maximum retry step limit and reflection/fallback loop.
Disable logging to reduce token count.
challenges.explanation: Production agents require loop breakers, max iteration limits, and reflection fallbacks.
